_note: Saltpetre and the nitrogen chain. Written at COST-STRUCTURE level only - what a process consumes and how much comes out - because that is what the price solver needs and it is all it needs. No procedure, no conditions, no operating detail. The economically interesting fact here is a calendar, not a recipe.

nitre_kg.extracted_from: nitre bed, or a mined deposit, or import
nitre_kg.basis: per tonne of refined saltpetre from a worked nitre bed
nitre_kg.yield_basis: THE COST HERE IS A CALENDAR, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE POINT. A nitre bed is soil, manure and ash left to nitrifying bacteria for 12 to 24 months. No amount of money shortens it, which is why this single material gates the entire nitrogen branch of the tech tree and why the simulator already models nitre beds as a calendar floor rather than a purchase. The mass ratio is poor - a bed yields a low single-digit percentage of its charge as nitre - and the labour is turning and leaching over two years rather than skilled work. The alternatives are geographic rather than technical: mined deposits where they exist, or import from the Gangetic plain along a route Rome already sails. A society with neither, and no patience, does not get nitrogen chemistry at all. Numbers are order of magnitude; the two-year floor is the number that matters and it is well attested.

capital.capital_basis: Nitre plantations were sheds of beds of manure, earth and ash turned and wetted for a year or two, then leached in vats and the lye boiled in iron cauldrons. Capacity is the staff's: the five or so hands a bed-yard keeps at the entry's four hundred and twenty labour-hours a tonne, about twenty tonnes a year. Masses are order-of-magnitude figures. PASS 9 (Complaint 671): en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potassium_nitrate (opened): a nitre-bed compost pile typically 4 ft high, 6 ft wide and 15 ft long (1.2 x 1.8 x 4.6 m, 10 m3), leached after about a year; beds of rotted manure and straw were wetted weekly and turned. 1911 Britannica Saltpetre and Nitre (opened) give no yield per bed or per year. Failing inputs: kilograms of nitre per bed (so the 20000 kg a year and the shed and vat masses are unbounded). Stays D. Wikipedia Nitre and Mining Bureau and a Confederate nitre search found no kilograms of nitre per bed. Still unsourced, so the row stays D: kg of nitre per bed, shed and vat masses, labour hours, life. PASS 13 (Complaint 671), still D. tried: (1) yield per bed: a reprint of LeConte's Confederate Nitre Bureau pamphlet (yeisenachitel.blogspot.com/2014/12/potassium-nitrate.html, opened) says writers vary from 15 to 60 lb of salt per cubic yard of nitrified earth, 8.9 to 35.6 kg/m3, so 20 t a year needs 560 to 2,250 m3 of earth leached a year; (2) bed time and layer from Ure (archive.org/stream/dictionaryofarts00urea, opened, article Nitrate of Potash): process lasts two years, layers 2 to 3 ft thick under sheds, Longchamp's sheds 130 x 30 ft; a bed of one to two years' stock is 560 to 4,500 m3, at 0.76 m a layer 740 to 5,900 m2 of floor, 2 to 16 Longchamp sheds of 362 m2; Wikipedia Potassium nitrate (opened) bed of 10 m3 gives 56 to 450 beds; (3) stand-in: France in the Revolution made 2,000 t a year of saltpetre (Ure), 100 times this row, for scale only. The shed count therefore spans a factor of 8 and the labour of the row (420 h a tonne) is not consistent with 100 or more beds turned weekly; no opened page gives timber per shed. Missing: timber and stone per square metre of nitre shed, and vat sizes.

nitre_kg.holding_basis: A nitre bed is left to ripen for a year or two before it is leached, so the manure and ash it was built from are tied up for about that long.

nitric_acid_kg.yield_basis: STOICHIOMETRIC, so the ratio follows from the molar masses rather than from an estimate: potassium nitrate is 101.1 g/mol and nitric acid 63.0, so a tonne of acid needs about 1.6 t of nitre at perfect conversion, and rather more in practice. Taken at 1.35 t here against a partial-conversion route that leaves a bisulphate rather than driving to completion. The economic point, and the only one the solver needs, is that nitric acid costs a nitre and a sulfuric acid - it inherits the two-year calendar of the first and the fuel of the second, which is why it stays expensive in any society that cannot do both. Cost structure only; this entry deliberately carries no process detail.

capital.capital_basis: Nitre and oil of vitriol were heated in rows of retorts in a galley furnace and the vapour collected in cooled receivers; twenty retorts charged twice a week is some forty tonnes of nitre a year, thirty tonnes of acid at the entry's yield; half is taken as the stated capacity. PASS 9 (Complaint 671): 1911 Britannica Nitric Acid (en.wikisource.org, opened) describes distilling saltpetre with sulphuric acid in horizontal cast iron stills, the vapours condensed in a series of stoneware Woulfe bottles; it gives no still size, charge weight or time, so the twenty retorts and the twice-weekly charge here are not bounded. Stays D. PASS 12 (Complaint 671), still D but bounded. Lunge, Sulphuric Acid and Alkali (https://archive.org/stream/manufacturesulp02lunggoog/manufacturesulp02lunggoog_djvu.txt, opened, chapter Nitric Acid, pp. 139 to 149): nitric acid was formerly made in glass retorts and is now made in cast-iron retorts; a Griesheim horizontal cylinder works off 8 cwt (406 kg) of nitre per 24 hours including filling and emptying (25 percent more in case of need) with 2.5 cwt of coal; a French cast-iron pot 4 to 5 ft across and as high, wall 1.5 to 2 in, takes 9 cwt (457 kg) of nitre and 16 to 18 hours (1 hour charging, 6 hours first stage, about 6 hours second stage, 4 to 5 hours last stage); a Valentiner vacuum pot takes a ton of nitre in 12 hours; sulphuric acid is used 20 to 30 percent above the equivalent. Scale check: the row's 40 t of nitre a year is 133 charges of 300 kg, about a third of one Griesheim cylinder's 122 t a year (406 kg x 300 days), so the row's capacity is one small furnace by the book's standard and its twice-weekly charge of about 19 kg per retort is not contradicted; 20 clay retorts holding 19 kg of nitre apiece is an unsourced geometry, and the sources describe iron, not clay, retorts for the acid. Still unsourced, so the row stays D: the clay or stoneware retort count and charge, and the galley's brickwork and stone mass. PASS 13 (Complaint 671), now C. Furnace from a comparable: Thorpe, A Dictionary of Applied Chemistry (archive.org/stream/b21713595_0003/b21713595_0003_djvu.txt, opened, article Phosphorus): a galley furnace for 24 retorts of 30 litres is 9.6 m3 of masonry (12.5 x 7 ft outside, 9 in walls, assumed 1.8 m wall height), 0.40 m3 a retort; the row's 20 retorts holding 19 kg of nitre (with acid about 35 L, an assumed fill) are 8.0 m3, 4,000 bricks at 504 a m3 (Wikipedia Fire brick, opened), set to 4 thousand brick and about 1 m3 of foundation stone, 2,500 kg at 2,400 kg/m3 (assumed), against the old 10 thousand and 5,000 kg. Hours: Colliery Engineer Co., Treatise on Architecture and Building Construction vol 4 (chestofbooks.com/architecture/Building-Construction-V4/Data-On-Brickwork.html and Data-On-Rubble-Masonry.html, opened): common brickwork takes bricklayer 7 h and laborer 7 h per 1,000 brick, a perch of rubble (0.708 m3) takes 1/3 mason-day and 1/4 helper-day; self-build.co.uk (already cited) gives 40 to 60 bricks an hour, so furnace brickwork is taken at the slow end, 25 h per 1,000, and rubble at 4.7 h/m3 (10 hour day assumed): 4,000 x 25 h per 1,000 = 100 h plus 1 m3 x 4.7 h = 105 h of mason; laborer 55 h (half, the self-build.co.uk ratio). Life: Lunge (archive.org/stream/manufacturesulp02lunggoog, opened, Nitric Acid): the Guttmann retort bench has the cylindrical middle 'practically for ever', bottoms up to ten years and covers about one year; a brick galley setting of 15 years is inside that bracket and kept.

Acid and heat crack retorts after a few dozen firings. PASS 9 (Complaint 671): no opened page gives the number of firings a nitric acid retort survives or its mass; the life of half a year and 2500 kg of clay are estimates. The Belgian zinc retort life of two to three weeks (US patent 2447369, opened) shows how short a hot-chemistry fireclay life can be, but it is a different charge. Stays D. PASS 12 (Complaint 671), still D. Lunge, Sulphuric Acid and Alkali (https://archive.org/stream/manufacturesulp02lunggoog/manufacturesulp02lunggoog_djvu.txt, opened, chapter Nitric Acid, pp. 139 to 149): nitric acid was formerly made in glass retorts and is now made in cast-iron retorts; a Griesheim horizontal cylinder works off 8 cwt (406 kg) of nitre per 24 hours including filling and emptying (25 percent more in case of need) with 2.5 cwt of coal; a French cast-iron pot 4 to 5 ft across and as high, wall 1.5 to 2 in, takes 9 cwt (457 kg) of nitre and 16 to 18 hours (1 hour charging, 6 hours first stage, about 6 hours second stage, 4 to 5 hours last stage); a Valentiner vacuum pot takes a ton of nitre in 12 hours; sulphuric acid is used 20 to 30 percent above the equivalent. Lunge gives no life or mass for earthenware nitric retorts (the trade had moved to iron, which lasts as long as the setting does since the fire gases surround the cylinder and no corrosion takes place); the half-year life and 2,500 kg of clay remain estimates. PASS 13 (Complaint 671), now C, life changed 0.5 -> 0.17. Mass: Wall thickness ratio: Thorpe retort for phosphorus is 8 in inside diameter, 3 ft long, clay about 1 in thick (Thorpe, A Dictionary of Applied Chemistry (archive.org/stream/b21713595_0003/b21713595_0003_djvu.txt, opened, article Phosphorus)); the row's 19 kg of nitre with its acid fills about 35 L (assumed), a retort 0.30 m across and 0.5 m long with a 35 mm wall (the same 1:8 ratio, rounded) has 0.8 m2 x 0.035 m x 2,000 kg/m3 (assumed clay density) = 56 kg; 20 retorts are 1,120 kg and 20 stoneware receivers at the Red Hill General Store crock rate (redhillgeneralstore.com/housewares/kitchen/kitacc/Ohio-Stoneware-Crocks.htm, opened: 0.45 kg a litre for a 10 gallon crock) of about 35 L each are 16 kg x 20 = 320 kg, 1,450 kg with spare against the row's 2,500 kg, within 1.7, kept. Life by firing count: Lunge (vitriol retorts, above) shows a fireclay retort in acid service lasting about 18 charges (Starck: 724,000 retorts a year over 120 furnaces of 306, one charge a day); the nitre retorts are charged twice a week (104 charges a year, the row's own basis), so 18 charges are 0.17 year; the Starck retorts run hotter than nitre retorts, so this is a lower figure. Potter hours: Deneen Pottery (deneenpottery.com/get-to-know-some-of-the-hands-that-make-your-mugs, opened) 300 mugs a day is about 120 kg of clay a day at an assumed 0.4 kg a mug; a third of that for retorts is 40 kg a day, 1,450 kg takes 36 days, 290 h against 250 h, kept.

nitrocellulose_kg.yield_basis: COST STRUCTURE ONLY. Nitrated cellulose gains mass over the cellulose it starts from, so the fibre input is well under a tonne; the acids are largely recovered and re-used rather than consumed, and the figures here are net of a recovery this entry does not attempt to model in detail. What the solver needs from this entry is that the cost is dominated by the nitric acid, which inherits saltpetre's two-year calendar, and not by the cellulose, which is rags. That is the fact that decides whether a society can afford the material at all. No procedure, conditions or operating detail is recorded here, deliberately.

nitroglycerin_kg.yield_basis: COST STRUCTURE ONLY, on the same pattern as nitrocellulose and for the same reason. Glycerol comes from fat as a by-product of soap making, so the organic input is cheap and abundant wherever soap is made; the acids dominate, and the nitric acid among them, so the cost again traces back through saltpetre to a two-year bed. The one economically distinctive fact is the handling: the product cannot be stored or carried like an ordinary industrial chemical, so its delivered cost carries a transport and loss penalty that the ordinary freight model will understate. Flagged here rather than modelled. No procedure, conditions or operating detail is recorded, deliberately.
